briefing.focus: Fairway-finder day. 139 slope, narrow and tree-lined — the mini driver and 2-iron are your scoring clubs off the tee, and bogey is never an emergency here.

sections.b: Mungeam design (2004) carved into a hillside: 6,935 yards, par 71, rating 73.7 / slope 139 from the tips — the longest, toughest, best-kept muni in Westchester. Narrow fairways lined with trees and fescue, elevated tees AND elevated greens, a few blind shots, and almost no flat lies. Front nine is an accuracy exam; back nine wants length and short game. Play the tees that match a 6,300–6,500 game, not the tips — the slope is real.

sections.t: Off the tee — your bag is built for this place
sections.b: This is exactly why you carry the r7 Mini and the 2-iron. Blind or squeezed landing area (the 2nd is famously tight, the 7th is a beast): mini driver (~220) or 2-iron (~205) and walk to the fairway. Save the Stealth 2 for the open, longer back-nine holes where the extra 15 yards matters. One rule all day: on any tee shot you can't fully see, take the club you'd bet $100 finds short grass.

sections.t: The lies are the hidden test
sections.b: Hillside course = sidehill everything. Ball above your feet wants to go LEFT — with your strong lofts, take one less club and aim right edge. Ball below feet pushes right; widen the stance and swing smooth. Uphill approach: club UP, always — elevated greens reject anything short and roll it 20 yards back down the hill. Short-siding yourself here is the double-bogey machine; center of every green is a genuinely good shot.

When you punch out or lay up, do it to YOUR numbers: 95 (full 56°) or 108 (full 50°) — not 'as far as possible' into an awkward half-shot from a sloped lie. On uphill wedges into elevated greens, the ball lands steep and stops fast: fly it to the flag.

sections.t: Greens — first real test for the DF3i
sections.b: Reviewers call them tour-fast. Perfect debut for the zero-torque: your job is speed only, the face is handled. Lag ladder mindset from 25+ feet — die everything into the 6-foot circle. Spend the first three greens calibrating pace, and on breaking putts play extra break with dying speed. Keep the low-through-impact feel from the gate drill: that is still your one open fault, and fast greens punish a popped stroke worst.

Extremely hilly — take the cart, save the legs for the back nine. July heat means carries play a touch longer (load the weather tile at the first tee — the ladder's Today column does the math). Target: doubles are the enemy, not bogeys. Count them; fewer than three doubles on a 139 slope is a won day. Log the round in Coach after — score, putts, and what bit you — and I'll debrief it against this plan.

briefing.focus: Conventional vs. left-hand-low vs. claw — decided by makes and miss direction, not feel. One stage at a time.

sections.t: Why your right hand is the suspect
sections.b: For a right-handed putter, the trail hand is the strong, dominant one — under pressure it wants to rotate and flip the face closed through impact, and a closed face is a pull left. That is literally what Session 1's frame-by-frame showed: toe-over rotation, varying rep to rep. Both alternative grips exist to take that rotation out of the stroke. The DF3i already removes most of the need — this experiment measures what's left.

CONVENTIONAL (reverse overlap): handle in the palms, palms parallel to the face, thumbs down the Press Pistol's flat front, pressure 3/10, right palm 'along for the ride.' LEFT-HAND-LOW: lead hand below trail — levels the shoulders and turns the stroke into a shoulder-rocked pendulum; the structural fix, and a natural pair with a straight SBST stroke. CLAW: normal left hand, right hand in a pencil/saw hold — the surgical 'delete the right hand' move; smallest change, shines inside 10 feet.

sections.t: Stage 0 — baseline the conventional grip FIRST (weeks 1–2)
sections.b: You just changed the two biggest levers (zero-torque head, lie). Roll the DF3i with your normal grip for two weeks: one 20-ball 5-footer test per week, tapped into the Putting Lab with miss directions. GATE: 2 or fewer left misses per 20 in both weeks → conventional wins, experiment over, don't add complexity to a solved problem. 3+ lefts in either week → advance to Stage 1.

sections.t: Stage 1 — the head-to-head (only if the gate trips)
sections.b: Practice-green session: alternate 10-ball blocks from 5 feet — conventional, LHL, claw, then repeat (60 balls, two blocks each). Log every block in the Decisions 10-ball tester named 'DF3i · conventional', 'DF3i · LHL', 'DF3i · claw' with miss pattern notes. Then add the lag check: 5 balls from 30 feet with each grip — average leave distance matters as much as makes, because alternative grips usually tax distance feel first. Two separate sessions minimum before any verdict.

Winner = most makes + fewest left misses across all blocks, with a lag leave you can live with. Commit to it for 3 full weeks before re-judging (every grip change feels bad for two weeks — that's adaptation, not information). Hybrid option is legitimate: conventional for lag, claw inside 10 feet, if the blocks split that way. Film one face-on session with the winner so the early-lift verdict lands on the final setup.

The Press Pistol 2° stays — flat-front, face-square-friendly, and its built-in forward press works for all three holds. The only future nudge if hands stay noisy: an oversized SuperStroke-style grip, which damps wrist rotation further. Later, only if the data asks for it.

sections.t: The setup constants — same for all three grips
sections.b: These never change during the experiment, so the grip is the only variable. BALL POSITION: one to two ball-widths inside your lead (left) heel — forward of center, so the DF3i meets the ball just past the low point with a slight upstroke for true roll (ball too far back = downward strike = the hop-and-skid your old thin contact hinted at). EYES: directly over the ball or a hair inside the line — run the nose-drop test once to set it (drop a ball from the bridge of your nose at address; it should land on the ball or just inside). STANCE: feet shoulder-width, knees soft, weight 55/45 favoring the lead side, and dead still — the stroke moves, the body doesn't. DISTANCE FROM BALL: arms hang straight down from the shoulders, no reaching — this also keeps the sole flat (the toe-up aim-left problem lives here). ALIGNMENT: square the face to your line FIRST, then build the stance around the face. PRESS: none added — the Press Pistol 2° has the forward lean built in; hands sit even with the ball.

sections.t: Grip 1 · Conventional (reverse overlap) — the exact hold
sections.b: LEFT HAND first, at the top: the handle runs up your LIFELINE (the crease between thumb pad and heel pad), NOT across the fingers like a full-swing grip — this locks the wrist. Left thumb flat, straight down the Press Pistol's flat front. RIGHT HAND below it: same palm placement — handle up the lifeline, right thumb flat down the front — so both PALMS FACE EACH OTHER, parallel to the putter face. They now work as one unit: if the palms oppose, the face can't rotate without both wrists agreeing. FINISH: lift your left index finger and lay it OVER the fingers of the right hand (across the pinky and ring finger) — that's the reverse overlap, and it further handcuffs the right wrist. Pressure 3/10, both hands. Feel: the back of the left hand IS the putter face — swing it at the target; the right palm just mirrors.

Everything mirrors: RIGHT HAND goes at the TOP now — handle up the right lifeline, right thumb flat down the front. LEFT HAND below it — handle up the left lifeline, left thumb down the front, palms opposing as always. OVERLAP: lay your right index finger over the fingers of the left hand (the mirror of reverse overlap). CRITICAL CHECKS: your shoulders should feel — and be — LEVEL at address (that's the whole point; the normal grip tilts the right shoulder down), and your LEFT wrist stays flat and leads the stroke like a paddle; the left hand going low turns your lead side into the engine and demotes the right hand to a passenger. Expect it to feel alien for two weeks and expect lag to suffer first — that's why the 30-foot check is in the protocol.

LEFT HAND: identical to conventional — top of the grip, up the lifeline, thumb down the front. This hand now does ALL the holding. RIGHT HAND: rotate it so the palm faces YOUR BODY (not the target), then hold the grip like a PENCIL — thumb pad resting on the back of the handle, the first two fingertips lying on the front/top. The handle sits in the notch between thumb and index finger. Pressure 2/10 — the right hand is a fairing, not a motor; it physically cannot rotate the face from that position, which is the entire trick. Right elbow drifts slightly away from your side — let it. Variation if the pencil feels twitchy: the SAW — same idea but all four right fingertips lie across the front of the grip like holding a saw handle. Either counts as 'claw' in the blocks; pick one and keep it.

detail.story: First measured block of the Grip Experiment, scored frame-by-frame from ten clips. Eight drops. The scoring learned this mat's behavior on the way: made balls fall through and auto-return the full length of the mat at steady speed (which is how putt 3 — initially scored short — was corrected to a make: gravity can't roll a ball six feet back up a flat mat). The two real misses share a signature: both balls DIED at the hole. One settled an inch to the pull side, one hung on the near-left lip. detail.compare: Versus the old baseline: the catastrophic left start line is gone. What's left is arrival-speed fine-tuning — a firmer 'back of the cup' pace would likely have converted both misses.
detail.limits: Ramped return mat punishes dying pace more than a real green (a real cup accepts soft-entry putts these lips rejected). 4-footers, not the protocol's 5 — still counts as Stage 0 evidence, but run the official 20-ball at 5 feet for the gate. Clips end at arrival, so 'vanish + full-length return' = make is the scoring rule.

briefing.course: Swing Focus — Hips & the Laid-Off Top
briefing.focus: Two swings filmed Jul 26 share two traits: good ground-up sequencing (keep) and a slightly across-the-line top (fix). sections.t: The one connection: laid-off top + stalled hips are the same story
sections.b: When the club gets across the line / laid off at the top (shaft pointing right of target, trail elbow drifting behind you), the downswing has to re-route the club to save the shot. The most common save is the hips SLIDING toward the target and the chest hanging back — which is precisely the 'great at the top, lose it through contact' feeling. So we don't chase two separate fixes: clean up the top so the hips don't have to bail you out, and train the hips to CLEAR (rotate open) instead of slide. Fix the cause, the symptom follows.

sections.t: What the film showed (both clubs, Jul 26)
sections.b: GOOD, protect it: full coil, head behind the ball (driver), lower-body-led transition on both, and a balanced held finish. WEDGE bonus: spine angle stayed, you covered the ball — a proper descending strike. TO FIX: (1) slightly across-the-line top on BOTH clubs — one feel fixes both; (2) driver hips look to slide level through impact instead of clearing up-and-around. sections.t: Fix 1 · Clean up the top (trail elbow in front)
sections.b: FEEL: at the top, the trail (right) elbow points more DOWN at the ground and stays in FRONT of your trail-hip seam, keeping the club a hair more in front of your chest. Right now the elbow drifts behind you, which lays the shaft off. DRILL — Split-hand / trail-arm-only: make slow half-swings feeling the trail elbow lead down into the slot; pause at the top and check the shaft points AT the target line, not right of it. Mirror or a phone on a tripod DTL at the top confirms it. 10 slow reps before you hit balls.

sections.t: Fix 2 · Clear the hips, don't slide them
sections.b: FEEL: from the top, the lead (left) hip clears BACK and UP — belt buckle turning left and rotating open — while your chest stays over the ball a beat longer. Not a slide toward the target; a turn around a post. This is where your speed and your 'through contact' consistency live. DRILLS: (a) Trail-foot-back / step-through: hit half wedges stepping the trail foot back through impact — forces rotation over slide. (b) Lead-hip-to-the-wall: set up with your lead hip a few inches off a wall/bag; on the downswing the hip should clear so it just brushes back and up, not bump forward into it. (c) Chair/impact-bag: feel the trail glute fire and the hips deepen (not thrust toward the ball) so you don't early-extend. 2–3 sets of 10 each, twice a week.

sections.t: Driver vs wedge — keep them different on purpose
sections.b: DRIVER: ball forward, hips clearing up-and-around so you hit slightly UP — that's carry and less spin. WEDGE: keep exactly what the film showed — stay down, cover the ball, hit DOWN; don't let 'clear the hips' turn into standing up out of a wedge. Same sequencing engine, opposite low-point. If a swing thought bleeds the wrong way, park it — the wedge is already good.

briefing.focus: Your WINNERSPIRIT Miracle 201 is the perfect home tool for the two things the Jul 26 film flagged: sequencing (hips lead) and releasing THROUGH contact instead of losing it. This is the standing at-home practice plan. Pairs with the Swing Focus plan.

sections.t: How the tool talks to you (read first)
sections.b: The Miracle 201 is a weighted (~550g), whippy carbon/glass-fiber trainer with TWO feedback channels. (1) THE CLICK: a slider fires an audible click at the point of maximum speed in your swing — WHERE you hear it tells you WHEN you're releasing. (2) THE SPEED DIAL: adjustable from ~15–50 m/s (≈34–111 mph); it sets how much speed is needed to trigger the click. Turn it DOWN for tempo work, UP to demand more clubhead speed or simulate a longer club. Because the shaft is heavy and flexible, you physically cannot rush it — it forces you to load and wait, which is exactly the medicine for your quick, across-the-line top.

Space: ~8 ft clear all around and a high ceiling (garage, basement with clearance, or backyard). Never near people, lights, or a TV. Hold it with your normal CONVENTIONAL grip and your real posture — this only transfers if the setup matches your actual swing. WARM UP FIRST: 20–30 slow, smooth swings before anything hard — at 550g it's heavier than your driver and a cold max swing is how you tweak a back or oblique. Do a few swings LEFT-handed too (opposite of normal) each session — it balances the body and builds the anti-rotation muscles that protect you.

Dial LOW. Make smooth 3:1 swings and FEEL the shaft bend and lag behind your hands at the top — if you snatch from the top it flails and clicks early/weak. Count 'one-and-… two': long patient load back, unhurried transition, then let it sling. This directly rewires the 'great at the top but quick coming down' pattern. 2 sets of 10, both directions. This is the most important drill on the list — do it every session.

sections.t: Drill 2 · Impact timing — make the CLICK fire PAST the ball
sections.b: This one targets your exact complaint: 'lose it through contact.' GOAL: the click should crack at the BOTTOM of the arc — at or just PAST your lead leg — not up in the downswing. An EARLY click = casting / throwing the release away before impact (all your speed spent above the ball). Keep the wrists hinged and let the head release LATE so the click fires down by where the ball would be. 3 sets of 8. Listen every rep and adjust until the click consistently lives at/after the bottom.

sections.t: Drill 3 · Transition & hips-lead (ties to Swing Focus)
sections.b: From the top, start down with the LOWER BODY — feel the lead hip clear BACK and UP while the trainer's head still lags behind. Because the head is heavy and slow to catch up, it exaggerates the hips-lead-hands feeling you need. If you spin the shoulders/arms first, the click comes early and weak — instant feedback that you cast. Do this right after the wall / trail-foot-back drills in your Swing Focus plan so the feel carries over. 2 sets of 8.

sections.t: Drill 4 · Top-of-swing check — kill the laid-off shaft
sections.b: Slow reps to a PAUSE at the top. Feel the trail (right) elbow point down and stay IN FRONT of your trail-hip seam — the whippy shaft makes an across-the-line/laid-off top feel obviously 'stuck' and off-plane, which a normal club hides. Check in a mirror or a phone on a tripod that the shaft points at the target line, not right of it. 10 slow reps, no speed — this is a position drill.

Dial UP. After a full warm-up: all-out swings for pure speed — at higher dial settings the click ONLY fires if you genuinely accelerate through the bottom. Protocol: 3 sets of 5 MAX-effort swings with full rest between sets (this is nervous-system/speed work — quality over quantity, never grind it into cardio). Throw in a few non-dominant-side swings. Benchmark: the highest dial setting you can consistently trigger — track it over weeks and watch it climb.

2–3 short sessions/week, 10–15 min each — and DON'T max out every time: alternate a TEMPO/TIMING day (Drills 1–4, low dial) with a SPEED day (Drill 5, high dial). Pre-round: 15–20 easy swings as a dynamic warm-up and tempo primer. Log in Coach: the dial setting you can reliably trigger, and whether the click is firing at/past the ball yet. Next time you film at the sim we'll check whether the later release and hips-lead carried into the real swing.

briefing.focus: A checkpoint map of WHERE the body goes — feet, knees, hips, spine, hands, head — from address to finish, so you can freeze each spot in a mirror or on video and match it. Built to answer 'where am I supposed to be?' — especially the hips (see the last two sections). RH references: LEAD = left, TRAIL = right.

sections.b: Don't try to hit all of these at once — that's paralysis. Pick ONE checkpoint per session, rehearse it slowly in a mirror (face-on) and on a down-the-line phone clip, then hit a few balls letting it happen. Positions are a map, not a swing thought for over the ball. Everything below is for a right-handed golfer: LEAD side = left, TRAIL side = right.

sections.t: 1 · Address — the setup everything else depends on
sections.b: FEET: shoulder-width for irons (insides of the heels about under your armpits), a touch wider for driver. Flare the LEAD foot out ~20–30° — this pre-clears room for the hips to turn through later. WEIGHT: 50/50 for irons, balanced on the arches (not toes, not heels); driver slightly on the trail side (~55/45). KNEES: soft athletic flex, like the top of a light squat — not locked, not deep. HIPS: hinge from the hip SOCKETS, not the waist — push your butt back like you're closing a car door with it. Pelvis neutral, hips level, small natural arch in the low back. SPINE/CHEST: tilt forward from that hinge so your chest is over the balls of your feet, plus a slight trail-shoulder-lower tilt (natural, since the trail hand sits lower on the grip). ARMS/HANDS: let the arms hang straight down from the shoulders — hands roughly under your chin, over your shoelaces. Irons: slight shaft lean, hands over the lead thigh. Driver: hands level with the ball. HEAD: steady, eyes down, chin UP off your chest so the lead shoulder can turn under it. BALL: driver off the lead heel; irons center to just right of center (your Golf Mind note).

sections.t: 2 · Takeaway — halfway back (club parallel to the ground)
sections.b: Move it back in ONE PIECE — hands, arms and chest turn together, no early wrist roll. FEET/KNEES: quiet; weight just starting to press into the trail heel. HIPS: barely rotating — the TRAIL hip is turning BEHIND you, not sliding out over the trail foot (that slide is a sway). CHECKPOINT: shaft parallel to the target line, toe pointing up, hands over the trail thigh, lead arm straight and still across the chest.

FEET: pressure loaded into the trail heel and instep; lead heel can stay down or lift slightly — either is fine. KNEES: the TRAIL knee HOLDS its address flex — if it straightens, you've swayed/stood up. HIPS: turned ~45° so your belt buckle points right of the ball, and you feel LOADED into the trail glute — like you're sitting into that right hip. Trail hip should still be inside the trail foot (outside it = sway). SPINE: same tilt you set at address, unchanged. SHOULDERS: turned ~90°, lead shoulder under the chin, upper back to the target — shoulders turn about twice as much as the hips (that gap is your coil). ARMS/HANDS: lead arm comfortably straight; TRAIL ELBOW points more DOWN at the ground and stays IN FRONT of the trail-hip seam (your working feel); shaft points at / parallel to the target line — not laid off across it. HEAD: still behind the ball, quiet.

sections.t: 4 · Transition — how the downswing STARTS (your problem spot)
sections.b: The ORDER is the whole game, and it runs ground-up WHILE the club is still finishing the backswing. (1) FEET/PRESSURE FIRST: press down into the LEAD foot — feel pressure move to the lead heel/instep. (2) HIPS SECOND: the LEAD hip then CLEARS — it rotates open (turns left) and back behind you and UP — while (3) the arms and club simply DROP into the slot (this is exactly your one-arm feel). You are NOT shoving the hips toward the target; you're turning them out of the way so the arms have room to fall. TRAIL SIDE: trail heel starts to lift, trail knee kicks in toward the lead knee. CHECKPOINT (down-the-line): when your hands reach hip height, the shaft should point at or just outside the ball and your hips are ALREADY opening. If the hands get to the ball before the hips have turned, you cast.

sections.t: 5 · Impact — the position all of it is for
sections.b: FEET: ~80–90% of pressure on the LEAD foot; trail foot up on the inside of the toe. LEAD LEG: straightening / 'posting up' — this extension pulls the hips up and around and is a big chunk of the speed you lose when you slide instead. HIPS: OPEN ~35–45° to the target — belt buckle already pointing LEFT of the ball, lead hip HIGH and behind you. SPINE/CHEST: still tilted, chest 'covering' the ball; for irons and wedges you stay DOWN through it. HANDS: ahead of the ball for irons (shaft lean, hands over the lead thigh); level for driver so you catch it slightly on the up. HEAD: still behind the ball, eyes down. This is the money frame — most of the checkpoints above exist only to get you here.

Keep rotating — the belt buckle turns from left-of-the-ball all the way to facing the target and past it. FEET: fully onto the lead foot, trail foot balanced on the toe with the laces to the target. HIPS: fully cleared and open, LEAD LEG tall and straight. CHEST: faces the target, then left of it. ARMS: extend down the line just after impact (the 'chase'), then fold up to a tall, balanced finish. Test: if you can HOLD the finish for 3 seconds without falling off balance, your sequence and weight shift were good.

sections.t: 7 · The HIPS in plain terms — SLIDE vs CLEAR (read twice)
sections.b: You're unsure here, so plainly: coming down, the hips can do two different things. A SLIDE is the hips moving SIDEWAYS toward the target — the belt buckle stays pointing at the ball, the hips stay 'closed,' and your upper body hangs back to counterbalance. That is the 'great at the top, lose it through contact' miss: no speed, hands flip to square the face, thin or fat strikes. A CLEAR (what you want) is the hips ROTATING — the lead hip turns back behind you and up as the lead leg straightens, so the belt buckle points LEFT of the ball at impact. THREE IMAGES that make it click: (a) There's a wall just behind your lead butt cheek — clearing = that cheek moves BACK to the wall, not toward the target. (b) You're standing in a barrel — you can TURN inside it but you can't slide out of it. (c) Pull your lead back pocket around behind you and up. Note: a SMALL lateral shift is real and necessary — but it happens in the FEET (pressure to the lead foot), and THEN the hips turn. Feet shift, hips spin — never the whole pelvis sliding as one block.

sections.t: 8 · How to groove it (feel beats positions)
sections.b: Positions are for the mirror; feels are for hitting. Best hip drills, all in your Swing Focus plan: TRAIL-FOOT-BACK step-through and LEAD-HIP-TO-THE-WALL — both make 'clear, don't slide' automatic because sliding is physically blocked. Then the ONE-HANDED Miracle 201 drop to feel the club fall while the hips open. Rehearse a checkpoint at ~50% speed until the shape is in; full speed returns on its own once the body trusts the position. One checkpoint at a time — stack them over weeks, not in one range session.

sections.b: The Miracle 201 is a weighted (~550g), whippy carbon/glass-fiber trainer with TWO feedback channels. briefing.focus: You feel better with the weight BACK while the ball sits off the front foot — and you've heard the weight is supposed to be forward. Here's what that combination actually costs you, why it lands squarely on the one putting fault still open on your card, and how to settle it with evidence instead of dogma.

sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the DF3i meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b: Ball off the FRONT foot is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b: Read the card. Path: settled. Face: settled. Start line: 10/10 clean, twice over. The ONE thing still open is pace — lags coming up short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, and both genuine misses in the Stage-0 4-footer block DIED at the hole. Hop-and-skid off a back-weighted low point is the textbook cause of exactly that signature. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Your strike quality might be.

Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.

sections.t: The third cost — the flip can come back
sections.b: Hanging back leaves the hands behind the ball through impact. Hands behind = the wrists want to save it = a flick. That flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. The DF3i's zero-torque head has buried that miss on film — but hands-behind is the one setup that can wake it up.

sections.t: Before changing anything — feel isn't real
sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. Weight that FEELS back is often pressure that's actually close to neutral — and neutral may be perfectly fine. Don't discard a setup you putt well from on the strength of a feel. FILM IT FACE-ON first. That single clip also closes the early-lift fault, the last open item from Session 8.

sections.t: What has to be true (the real checklist)
sections.b: Forget 'weight forward' as a slogan. Four things actually matter, and you can keep your comfort as long as they hold. (1) STERNUM at or just ahead of the ball. (2) HANDS level with or a touch ahead of the ball at impact — never behind it. (3) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the DF3i is a HAIR ascending at contact — that slight upstroke is what produces true roll. (4) PRESSURE around 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much that you start steering. If your weight-back feel still delivers 1 through 3, keep it.

sections.t: Settle it with data, not opinion
sections.b: A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: your current weight-back feel. Block B: 55/45 lead, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread. Tighter spread wins — that's the answer, not anyone's opinion. SOUND TEST: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a hopping ball adds a faint scuff a beat later — listen for the scuff. FACE-ON CLIP: check shaft lean at impact and where the head bottoms out relative to the ball.

The DF3i at 34" is zero-torque and heavy in the head — it squares itself and it wants to be swung, not steered. You can bias a touch more forward than feels natural without losing the feel you like. This putter absorbs the change better than a blade would.

sections.b: Ball position off the LEFT BREAST. Weight stacked right ON the ball. Normal address. Forward press right before contact, then putt. This supersedes the weight-back feel that started the conversation — the low point question is answered.

sections.t: Why the chest reference beats the foot reference
sections.b: You landed on 'left breast' rather than 'front heel,' and that's the better cue — keep it. The arc of a shoulder-rocked stroke is centered on your STERNUM, not your feet. Referencing the ball to your chest points it at the thing that actually governs the low point. Foot reference drifts every time your stance width changes by an inch; the chest reference doesn't. In putting posture those two land in roughly the same place anyway, so you've lost nothing and gained a cue that travels.

sections.t: Weight stacked on the ball — what that buys
sections.b: Pressure over the ball puts the sternum over or a whisker behind it, which pins the arc's bottom right where it belongs: at or just behind the ball, so the DF3i is a hair ascending at contact. That's the true-roll window. It's also why the setup 'feels good' — a pinned low point is what a repeatable strike feels like from the inside.

sections.t: The forward press — a TRIGGER, not a position
sections.b: This is a change from the static 'hands even, no press' note, and it's a legitimate one — because a press before contact does a different job than press held at address. Its purpose is to break inertia and start the stroke rhythmically instead of from a dead, frozen stop. Crenshaw, Nicklaus, half the great putters ever. Your tempo was a documented fault once (~1:1, fixed to 2.4:1 by the One-Two drill) — a press trigger is genuine maintenance for that.

sections.t: The one rule for the press
sections.b: SAME SIZE, EVERY TIME. The press changes the shaft lean, the shaft lean changes the effective loft, and the loft changes how far the ball rolls. A press that varies putt to putt is a loft that varies putt to putt — which is a PACE that varies putt to putt, and pace is the only fault still open on your card. Make it small, make it identical, and move it along the target line rather than hinging the wrists. The DF3i's zero-torque head protects the face; it can't protect you from a press that changes size.

sections.t: The routine as you described it
sections.b: 1) Line it up — read, aim the FACE first. 2) Set feet and hands, normal address. 3) Look at the hole. 4) Look at the aiming spot. 5) Look at the ball. 6) Forward press. 7) Putt. Structurally sound: face aimed before the stance gets built, an intermediate spot for line, one clear trigger to start it. Keep it brisk — three looks is the most you want before you go stale over the ball.

sections.t: THE GAP — nothing in this routine sets pace
sections.b: Read the seven steps again and ask what any of them does about how HARD you hit it. Nothing. Every step is aimed at LINE — the read, the face, the spot, the ball. And line is the part of your putting that's already settled: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. The one thing still broken is pace — lags short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, both Stage-0 misses dying at the hole. Your routine has no pace step in it at all.

sections.t: The fix — one rehearsal stroke, eyes on the hole

This is the single most reliable distance-control device there is: your eyes calibrate stroke size to distance far better than your conscious mind estimates it. Then look at the spot, look at the ball, press, go — pace is already loaded, and the last look is line. One rehearsal, not three.

On anything past ~25 feet, try keeping your eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke instead of returning them to the ball. It feels absurd and it is remarkably effective for distance — the ball isn't moving, you don't need to watch it. Test it as a block, not mid-round: 10 lags eyes-on-ball vs 10 eyes-on-hole, measure the spread of stopping points. Same measurement protocol as the weight A/B.

Your Golf Mind putting note still reads 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' That was written about the static address position and it's still true there — but it now sits awkwardly next to a deliberate press trigger. They're compatible (address neutral, press to start), just say so in the note so future-you doesn't read it as a contradiction.

Those two holes alone account for +10 of your +37, across just 6 of 45 holes played. Roughly a quarter of everything you lost came from two holes you played six times. If you get another crack at Wianno, they are the entire prep list.

8 par-5 plays: four bogeys, four pars, ZERO birdies. +4 total. Par 5s are supposed to be where a mid-single-digit makes his money, and you didn't convert one all week. Your wedge ladder off the 44° PW (60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122) exists precisely so the third shot into a par 5 is a number rather than a guess — decide the lay-up yardage from the ladder rather than hitting it as far as it goes.

These were matches, so some of these scores are most-likely-score postings rather than holed-out strokes. That mostly affects the doubles — a picked-up hole posts as a net double. The trend and the opening-hole pattern hold regardless, but don't read the double count as gospel on any single hole.
